summary.text:
The identity \(k inom{N+k-1}{k}=N inom{N+k-1}{k-1}\) removes the outer division and gives a summand \(C^3+2C^2D\), after which the one-step difference for \(N=pM\) is split into indices prime to \(p\) and indices \(pj\). Harmonic-sum bounds \(\sum_{p
mid h}h^{-2}\in p^e\mathbb Z_{(p)}\) and \(\sum_{p
mid h}h^{-1}\in p^{2e}\mathbb Z_{(p)}\), derived from sums over units modulo \(p^e\), reflection, and summation by parts, control the first part; for multiples of \(p\), expanding the binomial scaling factor \(\prod_{p
mid h}(1+pM/h)\) through quadratic order and combining these bounds with the valuation of the old summand makes the difference divisible by \(p^{3r}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(N)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^N(N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}\qquad(N\geq 1).
\]
Fix a prime \(p\geq5\). We prove that, for positive integers \(n,r\),
\[
 a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

Throughout, \(v_p\) denotes the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rational numbers. It is convenient to write
\[
 x=O(p^e)
\]
for a rational number \(x\) if either \(x=0\), or \(v_p(x)\geq e\). We repeatedly use the elementary rules
\[
 O(p^e)+O(p^e)=O(p^e),\qquad O(p^e)O(p^f)=O(p^{e+f}),
\]
and the fact that division by an integer not divisible by \(p\) does not alter such a bound. For an integer \(z\), the assertion \(z=O(p^e)\) is exactly \(p^e\mid z\).

Define, for \(N,k>0\),
\[
 C_{N,k}=\binom{N+k-1}{k},\qquad
 D_{N,k}=\binom{N+k-1}{k-1},
\]
and
\[
 T(N,k)=C_{N,k}^3+2C_{N,k}^2D_{N,k}.
\]
The standard adjacent-binomial identity gives
\[
 kC_{N,k}=ND_{N,k}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 (N+2k)C_{N,k}^3
 =NC_{N,k}^3+2C_{N,k}^2(kC_{N,k})
 =N\bigl(C_{N,k}^3+2C_{N,k}^2D_{N,k}\bigr).
\]
The term with \(k=0\) in the numerator defining \(a(N)\) is \(N\). Thus division by \(N\) may be performed term by term, and
\[
 a(N)=1+\sum_{k=1}^N T(N,k).                              \tag{2}
\]
This also directly proves the needed integrality of the defining quotient.

We now develop the harmonic-sum estimates used below. For \(L\geq0\), put
\[
 U_p(L)=\{k:1\leq k\leq L,\ p\nmid k\}.
\]

### 1. Complete reduced-residue reciprocal-square sums

For every positive \(E\),
\[
 \sum_{k\in U_p(p^E-1)}\frac1{k^2}=O(p^E).                \tag{3}
\]
To prove this, work first modulo \(q=p^E\). The elements \(1\leq k<q\) not divisible by \(p\) are precisely the units modulo \(q\). If
\[
 S=\sum_{u\in(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times}u^2,
\]
then multiplication by \(2\) permutes the units, so \(S=4S\). Since \(p\geq5\), the element \(3\) is invertible modulo \(q\), and hence \(S=0\pmod q\).

Inversion also permutes the units. Therefore the sum of the squares of the inverse residues is likewise zero modulo \(q\). For each \(k\in U_p(q-1)\), choose its inverse representative \(u_k\), with \(0\leq u_k<q\). Since \(ku_k\equiv1\pmod q\),
\[
 \frac1{k^2}-u_k^2=\frac{1-(ku_k)^2}{k^2}=O(p^E),
\]
because \(p\nmid k\). Summing this identity and using
\(\sum u_k^2\equiv0\pmod q\) proves (3).

A block version follows. If \(p^s\mid a\), then
\[
 \sum_{k\in U_p(pa-1)}\frac1{k^2}=O(p^{s+1}).             \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, write \(a=p^sb\) and \(q=p^{s+1}\). Every \(k\in U_p(qb-1)\) has a unique expression
\[
 k=tq+u,\qquad 0\leq t<b,\quad u\in U_p(q-1).
\]
Since \(p\nmid u\),
\[
 \frac1{(tq+u)^2}-\frac1{u^2}=O(p^{s+1}).
\]
Thus each block is congruent modulo \(p^{s+1}\) to the complete sum (3), and (4) follows.

We also need a stronger estimate for first reciprocals. If \(a>0\) and \(p^s\mid a\), then
\[
 \sum_{k\in U_p(pa-1)}\frac1k=O\bigl(p^{2(s+1)}\bigr).   \tag{5}
\]
Set \(L=pa\),
\[
 H=\sum_{k\in U_p(L-1)}\frac1k,
 \qquad
 K=\sum_{k\in U_p(L-1)}\frac1{k(L-k)}.
\]
The set \(U_p(L-1)\) is invariant under \(k\mapsto L-k\), because \(p\mid L\). Pairing the two reciprocal sums gives
\[
 2H=LK.                                                    \tag{6}
\]
For each admissible \(k\), both \(k\) and \(L-k\) are prime to \(p\), and
\[
 \frac1{k(L-k)}+\frac1{k^2}
 =\frac{L}{k^2(L-k)}=O(p^{s+1}),
\]
because \(p^{s+1}\mid L\). Summing and applying (4) shows \(K=O(p^{s+1})\). Since also \(L=O(p^{s+1})\), (6) gives \(2H=O(p^{2(s+1)})\). Finally, \(2\) is a \(p\)-adic unit, proving (5).

### 2. Binomial product formulas

For nonnegative integers \(N,k\),
\[
 \binom{N+k}{k}=\prod_{h=1}^k\frac{N+h}{h}.               \tag{7}
\]
Separating factors whose indices are multiples of \(p\) gives, for \(M,j\geq0\),
\[
 \binom{pM+pj}{pj}
 =\binom{M+j}{j}
   \prod_{h\in U_p(pj)}\left(1+\frac{pM}{h}\right).      \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, the factor with \(h=pq\) is \((pM+pq)/(pq)=(M+q)/q\), and their product is \(\binom{M+j}{j}\); the remaining factors are those displayed.

A shifted form will also be needed. If \(1\leq i\leq p\), then
\[
 \binom{pM+(pa+i)-1}{pa+i-1}
 =\binom{M+a}{a}
   \prod_{h\in U_p(pa+i-1)}\left(1+\frac{pM}{h}\right).  \tag{9}
\]
The multiples of \(p\) up to \(pa+i-1\) are exactly \(p,2p,\ldots,pa\), which proves the formula by the same separation.

Suppose now that \(r>0\) and
\[
 p^{r-1}\mid M.                                           \tag{10}
\]
Then \(pM=O(p^r)\). Every factor \((pM)/h\) in (9) is \(O(p^r)\), because \(p\nmid h\). Expanding the product, or inducting on the number of factors, shows that its difference from \(1\) is \(O(p^r)\). Hence
\[
 \binom{pM+(pa+i)-1}{pa+i-1}
 -\binom{M+a}{a}=O(p^r)                                  \tag{11}
\]
for \(1\leq i\leq p\).

We will also use the second-order expansion
\[
 \prod_h(1+x_h)
 =1+S_1+\frac{S_1^2-S_2}{2}+O(p^{3e}),                   \tag{12}
\]
whenever every \(x_h=O(p^e)\), where
\[
 S_1=\sum_hx_h,\qquad S_2=\sum_hx_h^2.
\]
This is just the expansion into elementary symmetric functions: the degree-one part is \(S_1\), and the degree-two part is
\(\sum_{h<\ell}x_hx_\ell=(S_1^2-S_2)/2\); every term of degree at least three is \(O(p^{3e})\). Equivalently, (12) follows by induction on the number of factors. Division by \(2\) is harmless since \(p\geq5\).

### 3. A weighted reciprocal-square sum

Under (10), with \(M>0\), we claim
\[
 \sum_{\substack{1\leq k<pM\\p\nmid k}}
 \frac{\binom{pM+k-1}{k-1}^{3}}{k^2}=O(p^r).             \tag{13}
\]
Partition the admissible indices uniquely as
\[
 k=pa+i,
 \qquad 0\leq a<M,\quad 1\leq i\leq p-1.
\]
Put
\[
 D_k=\binom{pM+k-1}{k-1},\qquad E_a=\binom{M+a}{a}.
\]
By (11), \(D_k-E_a=O(p^r)\). Therefore
\[
 D_k^3-E_a^3=(D_k-E_a)(D_k^2+D_kE_a+E_a^2)=O(p^r).
\]
Since \(p\nmid k\), replacing \(D_k^3\) by \(E_a^3\) in (13) creates only an \(O(p^r)\) error. It remains to prove
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^{M-1}E_a^3
 \sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\frac1{(pa+i)^2}=O(p^r).                \tag{14}
\]
Define
\[
 G(a)=\sum_{k\in U_p(pa-1)}\frac1{k^2}.
\]
The inner sum in (14) is \(G(a+1)-G(a)\), so the left side of (14) is
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^{M-1}E_a^3\bigl(G(a+1)-G(a)\bigr).           \tag{15}
\]
Discrete summation by parts gives
\[
 (15)=E_{M-1}^3G(M)
 +\sum_{a=0}^{M-2}(E_a^3-E_{a+1}^3)G(a+1),               \tag{16}
\]
because \(G(0)=0\).

The endpoint is \(O(p^r)\): by (10), formula (4) with \(s=r-1\) gives \(G(M)=O(p^r)\).

For an interior term, put \(s=v_p(a+1)\). Formula (4) gives
\[
 G(a+1)=O(p^{s+1}),
\]
so
\[
 \frac{G(a+1)}{a+1}=O(p).                                 \tag{17}
\]
The adjacent-binomial recurrence gives
\[
 E_{a+1}-E_a=\frac{M E_a}{a+1}.                           \tag{18}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 (E_a^3-E_{a+1}^3)G(a+1)
 =-E_a(E_a^2+E_aE_{a+1}+E_{a+1}^2)
   M\frac{G(a+1)}{a+1}.
\]
Here \(M=O(p^{r-1})\), while the final quotient is \(O(p)\) by (17). Thus every interior term is \(O(p^r)\). This proves (14), and hence (13).

### 4. Terms whose index is not divisible by \(p\)

Let
\[
 X=pM.
\]
By (10), \(X=O(p^r)\). For \(p\nmid k\), identity (1) gives
\[
 C_{X,k}=\frac{X D_{X,k}}k.
\]
Therefore
\[
 T(X,k)
 =\frac{X^3D_{X,k}^3}{k^3}
  +2\frac{X^2D_{X,k}^3}{k^2}.                            \tag{19}
\]
Summing over \(1\leq k<X\) with \(p\nmid k\), the first sum is termwise \(O(p^{3r})\). By (13), the sum occurring in the second part after removing the factor \(2X^2\) is \(O(p^r)\), so the second part is also \(O(p^{3r})\). Hence
\[
 \sum_{\substack{1\leq k<X\\p\nmid k}}T(X,k)
 =O(p^{3r}).                                               \tag{20}
\]
The endpoint \(k=X\) is divisible by \(p\), so this covers all nonmultiples of \(p\) among \(1,\ldots,X\).

### 5. Comparison of the terms at indices divisible by \(p\)

We next prove, for every \(j>0\),
\[
 T(pM,pj)-T(M,j)=O(p^{3r}).                               \tag{21}
\]
Let
\[
 v=v_p(j),\qquad
 S=U_p(pj-1),
\]
and define
\[
 R=\prod_{h\in S}\left(1+\frac{X}{h}\right),\qquad X=pM.
\]
(The set \(U_p(pj)\) is the same as \(U_p(pj-1)\), since \(pj\) itself is excluded.) Also set
\[
 H_1=\sum_{h\in S}\frac1h,
 \qquad H_2=\sum_{h\in S}\frac1{h^2},
\]
\[
 S_1=XH_1,
 \qquad S_2=X^2H_2.
\]
Because \(p^v\mid j\), estimates (5) and (4) give
\[
 H_1=O\bigl(p^{2(v+1)}\bigr),\qquad
 H_2=O(p^{v+1}).                                          \tag{22}
\]
Since \(X=O(p^r)\),
\[
 S_1=O\bigl(p^{r+2(v+1)}\bigr),\qquad
 S_2=O\bigl(p^{2r+v+1}\bigr).                            \tag{23}
\]
Applying (12) to \(x_h=X/h\),
\[
 R-1-S_1-\frac{S_1^2-S_2}{2}=O(p^{3r}).                  \tag{24}
\]
Moreover, from (23),
\[
 \frac{S_1^2-S_2}{2}=O\bigl(p^{2r+v+1}\bigr).            \tag{25}
\]

We also need a lower bound for \(T(M,j)\). Put
\[
 C=\binom{M+j-1}{j},\qquad D=\binom{M+j-1}{j-1}.
\]
If \(v<r-1\), then (1), namely \(jC=MD\), and \(M=O(p^{r-1})\) imply
\[
 C=O(p^{r-1-v}).
\]
Since
\[
 T(M,j)=C^2(C+2D),
\]
we obtain
\[
 T(M,j)=O\bigl(p^{2(r-1-v)}\bigr).                        \tag{26}
\]
If \(v\geq r-1\), we use only the trivial bound \(T(M,j)=O(1)\).

Combining (23), (25), and (26), with a case split, gives
\[
 S_1T(M,j)=O(p^{3r}),
\qquad
 \frac{S_1^2-S_2}{2}T(M,j)=O(p^{3r}).                    \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, if \(v<r-1\), the exponents in the first product add to
\[
 r+2(v+1)+2(r-1-v)=3r,
\]
and those in the second add to at least \(3r\). If \(v\geq r-1\), the factors \(S_1\) and \((S_1^2-S_2)/2\) themselves are already \(O(p^{3r})\). Multiplying (24) by the integral quantity \(T(M,j)\), and then using (27), yields
\[
 (R-1)T(M,j)=O(p^{3r}).                                   \tag{28}
\]
Since \(R=1+O(p^r)\), the factor \(R^2+R+1\) is \(O(1)\). Therefore
\[
 (R^3-1)T(M,j)
 =(R-1)(R^2+R+1)T(M,j)=O(p^{3r}).                         \tag{29}
\]

It remains to identify this expression with the left side of (21). Formula (8) says
\[
 \binom{pM+pj}{pj}=R\binom{M+j}{j}.                       \tag{30}
\]
The standard adjacent-binomial identities imply
\[
 \binom{pM+pj-1}{pj}=R\binom{M+j-1}{j},
\]
and
\[
 \binom{pM+pj-1}{pj-1}=R\binom{M+j-1}{j-1}.              \tag{31}
\]
For completeness, these follow by multiplying the first respective binomial in (31) by \(p(M+j)\): on the left one obtains respectively \(pM\binom{pM+pj}{pj}\) and \(pj\binom{pM+pj}{pj}\); after using (30), the common factor \(p\) cancels and the corresponding identities at scale \(M,j\) give (31). Thus both \(C\) and \(D\) in the definition of \(T\) are multiplied by \(R\) under \((M,j)\mapsto(pM,pj)\). Since \(T\) is homogeneous of degree three in \(C,D\),
\[
 T(pM,pj)=R^3T(M,j).
\]
Now (29) proves (21).

### 6. Completion of the one-step congruence

Partition the positive indices \(1\leq k\leq pM\) according as \(p\nmid k\) or \(p\mid k\). Every index in the second class has the unique form \(k=pj\), with \(1\leq j\leq M\). By (20) and (21),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\left(1+\sum_{k=1}^{pM}T(pM,k)\right)
 -\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{M}T(M,j)\right)\\
 &\quad=
 \sum_{\substack{1\leq k<pM\\p\nmid k}}T(pM,k)
 +\sum_{j=1}^{M}\bigl(T(pM,pj)-T(M,j)\bigr)
 =O(p^{3r}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (2), this says
\[
 a(pM)-a(M)=O(p^{3r}),
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
 a(pM)\equiv a(M)\pmod{p^{3r}},                           \tag{32}
\]
provided \(M>0\) and \(p^{r-1}\mid M\).

Finally take
\[
 M=np^{r-1}.
\]
It is positive, it is divisible by \(p^{r-1}\), and
\[
 pM=np^r.
\]
Substitution into (32) gives exactly
\[
 \boxed{a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r}}}.
\]
This holds for every positive \(n,r\) and every prime \(p\geq5\), as required.
